scribe_response.text: Tell me about a friend from when you were young. My dearest friend when I was young was a girl called Teresita, but everyone called her Tess. She lived four houses away, in a blue shack with a mango tree in the yard. We met when I was seven, the day she fell into the river. I fished her out with a bamboo pole, though the water only reached her waist. She screamed beautifully anyway, and afterward she said I had saved her life. I never denied it, because it made me feel like a uh hero. Tess was small and quick, with a gap in her teeth and scabbed knees. She could whistle through that gap better than any boy in the neighborhood. Every afternoon we collected shells along the riverbank and traded them like coins. She taught me to catch crabs with a string and a piece of fish head. I taught her to read, using labels from tin cans because her house had no books. Her mother sold fish at the uh market, and her hands always uh smelled of salt. Tess was embarrassed by that smell, but, but I told her I loved it. On Saturdays we helped our mothers, and afterward we made dolls uh from corn husks. What happened next? Tess was the better artist, and she drew tiny faces with a burnt matchstick. My dolls always looked angry, so we pretended they were the teachers. Under the big mango tree, the roots made a secret little room. We kept a biscuit tin um there, filled with shells, a blue marble, and a um letter. We promised to open the tin when we were old women. Tess wanted to be a singer, and she practiced with a coconut shell for a microphone. I wanted to be a teacher, and I practiced on her with great success. When we were twelve, her family moved to Bacolod, where her uncle had found work. I remember the morning they left, with their belongings piled on a truck. Tess stood at the back and waved her scarf until it turned the corner. I ran after it for a block um and lost one slipper. For months afterward the riverbank um felt empty, and even the shells seemed dull. We uh wrote letters for a while, with drawings in the margins and pressed flowers inside. Then life grew busy, the letters came less often, and finally they stopped. Can you tell me more about that? It is a small sadness that um I carry quietly, like a stone in a pocket. Years later, when I was already teaching, I received a postcard with a picture of a um stage. On the back she wrote that she had become a singer after all, but only in church. I laughed and cried at once, because that was exactly right. I never learned whether she opened the tin um under the mango tree. When I visited Iloilo again, the tree was gone, and a concrete house stood there. I stood um on the pavement for a long time, feeling foolish and tender. Now I sing in my own church choir in Abu Dhabi, and sometimes I think of her. When the sopranos, sopranos reach a high note, I imagine her whistling through that gap. A childhood friend knows the girl you were before you learned to be careful. Tess knew me when I was brave, silly, and barefoot. If she ever hears this story, I want her to know I kept the uh blue marble. I keep it in a dish beside my sewing box, and it catches the morning light. Good friends can be lost without ever really um being lost. I believe she is out there somewhere, still singing.
